# T32 — Systematic testing and debugging

| Track | Status | Hours | Dependency profiles |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cross-track | core | 69 | A, B, C |

**Prerequisites:** [T07](#t07), [T12](#t12), [T18](#t18).

| Reading | Implementation | Verification | Assessment | Consolidation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 30 | 16 | 8 | 5 |

## Purpose and outcomes

Build evidence that survives changes to implementation and environment. Testing progresses from independent contract oracles to model histories, fuzz/failure campaigns, supported instrumentation and reproducible diagnosis.

## Entry check and remediation

Write normal/boundary/invalid cases for a caller-storage component and explain output ownership after failure. Repair T07/T12/T18 interface/lifetime skills selectively. Confirm a supported Linux environment for Valgrind and GCC condition coverage; tool absence must be resolved for the dependent activity rather than treated as a pass.

Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for the diagnostic policy and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route order. Only the stated prelude leaves must precede a dependent project.

## Study sequence and teaching


<a id="t32-01"></a>

### T32.01 — Test architecture

A test architecture separates a portable contract from adapters and the harness that observes it. The harness may allocate and print even when the component is profile B/C. Build a caller-owned bounded queue/parser with a scripted adapter and a genuinely independent list/grammar oracle. A mock's deterministic convenience can hide physical side effects. Evidence is the dependency boundary, fixture manifest and a map of which properties need real OS/target execution.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-01-a"></a>


- **T32.01.a** Separate production components from test harness and platform adapters. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-01-b"></a>


- **T32.01.b** Define fixtures, deterministic inputs, and independent oracles. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-01-c"></a>


- **T32.01.c** Audit dependencies introduced solely by verification tooling. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-02"></a>

### T32.02 — Unit testing

Unit tests should observe contracts rather than struct layout. Partition empty, full, normal, invalid and failure cases; sentinel storage detects unintended writes outside the declared extent. Implement table-driven tests for a component's public API and critical invariants. Merely obtaining the expected return value does not establish preserved ownership or unchanged output on failure. Evidence includes both result checks and state/effect checks, with the smallest reproducer retained.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-02-a"></a>


- **T32.02.a** Test public contracts and critical internal invariants. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-02-b"></a>


- **T32.02.b** Cover boundaries, invalid input, empty states, and failure returns. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-02-c"></a>


- **T32.02.c** Avoid tests coupled unnecessarily to one implementation layout. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-03"></a>

### T32.03 — Integration and system testing

An integration test crosses an actual boundary: framing to partial I/O, driver to adapter, or application to shutdown logic. Reuse vectors while substituting scripted and real backends, but retain backend-specific expectations. A simulated successful write is not evidence of Linux short-I/O or physical UART behavior. Evidence is a complete acquisition-to-release workflow with partial progress, one failure and deterministic cleanup, plus a declared environment scope.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-03-a"></a>


- **T32.03.a** Verify contracts across real component boundaries. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-03-b"></a>


- **T32.03.b** Exercise backend substitution and complete operational workflows. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-03-c"></a>


- **T32.03.c** Distinguish mocked behavior from target or OS behavior. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-01](#pr-t32-01).


<a id="t32-04"></a>

### T32.04 — Property and model-based testing

Model-based testing generates operation sequences and compares implementation state to a simpler model after every operation. For a bounded queue, the list oracle is intentionally unlike a ring's index arithmetic. Enumerate short push/pop sequences and add seeded longer runs; minimize the first failing prefix. Random volume does not replace a stated invariant. Retain the seed, sequence and model/implementation disagreement, including a wraparound and full-queue case.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-04-a"></a>


- **T32.04.a** Generate operation sequences against a simpler reference model. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


<a id="t32-04-b"></a>


- **T32.04.b** State invariants independently of implementation code. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


<a id="t32-04-c"></a>


- **T32.04.c** Preserve seeds and minimize failing sequences. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


<a id="t32-05"></a>

### T32.05 — Differential and metamorphic testing

Differential testing is useful only when both implementations share the same contract; two copies of the same algorithm are weak independence. Metamorphic relations can supply checks without a complete expected output: scaling a linear FIR input scales its output, and splitting a stream into chunks preserves stateful results. Apply relations to the supplied filter/queue data and include a transformation that is intentionally invalid for saturation. Evidence explains why each relation holds and the assumptions it needs.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-05-a"></a>


- **T32.05.a** Compare independent implementations where valid references exist. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


<a id="t32-05-b"></a>


- **T32.05.b** Define transformations with predictable relationships between outputs. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


<a id="t32-05-c"></a>


- **T32.05.c** Detect shared assumptions that invalidate apparent oracle independence. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-02](#pr-t32-02).


<a id="t32-06"></a>

### T32.06 — Fuzzing

A fuzz harness takes bytes, bounds memory/work, resets state and avoids nondeterministic external effects. Start with valid short packets and malformed length/truncation seeds, then mutate deterministic bytes and persist the smallest failing case. Code coverage feedback is optional machinery, not the oracle. Evidence includes maximum input/work limits, timeouts, corpus identities and crash-versus-contract-failure triage; a clean campaign establishes only its explored execution scope.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-03](#pr-t32-03).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-06-a"></a>


- **T32.06.a** Build bounded, deterministic parser or component harnesses. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-03](#pr-t32-03).


<a id="t32-06-b"></a>


- **T32.06.b** Seed corpora with meaningful valid and malformed cases. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-03](#pr-t32-03).


<a id="t32-06-c"></a>


- **T32.06.c** Triage crashes and maintain minimized regression inputs. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-03](#pr-t32-03).


<a id="t32-07"></a>

### T32.07 — Fault injection

Failure injection turns hidden cleanup paths into controlled contracts. Number acquisition points and fail each in turn; for I/O also inject zero progress, partial progress and timeout. A callback returning an invalid count must be contained before pointer arithmetic uses it. Implement rollback with an observable live-resource ledger. Evidence requires every prefix to release only acquired resources and leave the caller's output in the declared failure state.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-04](#pr-t32-04).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-07-a"></a>


- **T32.07.a** Inject allocation, I/O, timeout, and partial-progress failures. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-04](#pr-t32-04).


<a id="t32-07-b"></a>


- **T32.07.b** Exercise every acquisition and rollback boundary. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-04](#pr-t32-04).


<a id="t32-07-c"></a>


- **T32.07.c** Test misbehaving adapters while stating actual isolation limits. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-04](#pr-t32-04).


<a id="t32-08"></a>

### T32.08 — Dynamic instrumentation

Dynamic tools have different detection mechanisms and environments. Compare a native ASan/UBSan build with an unsanitized debug binary under Valgrind Memcheck on a supported Linux setup; include heap overrun, use-after-free and an uninitialized value used in a branch. ASan alone is not an initialized-value detector. Also scope separate thread instrumentation where supported. Record reports, runtime/stack dependencies and slowdowns; an unsupported host is a route-to-supported-environment issue, not a passing test.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-08-a"></a>


- **T32.08.a** Apply address, undefined-behavior, thread, and memory-initialization checks where supported. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


<a id="t32-08-b"></a>


- **T32.08.b** Understand added runtime, memory, and execution costs. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


<a id="t32-08-c"></a>


- **T32.08.c** Document unsupported targets and incompatible instrumentation combinations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


<a id="t32-09"></a>

### T32.09 — Static analysis

Warnings and static analysis inspect executions through models and approximations. Run high-value compiler diagnostics and Eva or another supported path-sensitive analyzer on a bounded routine, then classify alarms by actual preconditions and configuration. Suppress only with a written contract argument and a regression test. Removing an alarm by assuming the failing input away changes the claim. Evidence includes the before/after code, analyzer configuration and the remaining uncertainty.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-09-a"></a>


- **T32.09.a** Combine compiler warnings with path-sensitive or abstract analysis. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


<a id="t32-09-b"></a>


- **T32.09.b** Review findings against contracts and configuration assumptions. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


<a id="t32-09-c"></a>


- **T32.09.c** Track justified suppressions and analysis regressions. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-05](#pr-t32-05).


<a id="t32-10"></a>

### T32.10 — Coverage

Coverage counts execution events, not correctness. For decision allow=length_ok && authorized, use TT, FT and TF to show each condition independently changes the decision while the other is fixed. Build a targeted MC/DC evidence table and compare statement, branch and condition-tool reports; short-circuit evaluation may leave a condition unevaluated. Evidence includes the independent-effect pairs and unreachable/excluded rationale. A 100% branch report alone is not this MC/DC argument.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-10-a"></a>


- **T32.10.a** Distinguish statement, branch, condition, path, and MC/DC objectives. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


<a id="t32-10-b"></a>


- **T32.10.b** Verify tool support and explain unreachable or excluded code. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


<a id="t32-10-c"></a>


- **T32.10.c** Avoid equating executed code with tested correctness. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


<a id="t32-11"></a>

### T32.11 — Mutation testing

Mutation testing asks whether an oracle notices meaningful wrong behavior. Change <= to < at a capacity boundary, omit a cleanup and invert authorization; run retained tests and explain survivors. Some mutations are equivalent under the declared domain and require reasoning rather than arbitrary new cases. Evidence distinguishes equivalent, killed, surviving and unexecuted mutations, and strengthens one previously weak oracle without coupling it to internal implementation details.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-11-a"></a>


- **T32.11.a** Select meaningful fault models and surviving mutations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


<a id="t32-11-b"></a>


- **T32.11.b** Diagnose weak oracles and untested error paths. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


<a id="t32-11-c"></a>


- **T32.11.c** Separate equivalent mutations from actual testing deficiencies. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-06](#pr-t32-06).


<a id="t32-12"></a>

### T32.12 — Interactive debugging

Interactive debugging should discriminate hypotheses. Reduce the input, state a predicted register/memory observation, set a breakpoint/watchpoint and test it before changing several variables. Compare debug and optimized builds with matching symbols; concurrent stepping changes timing. Evidence is a short hypothesis log with one rejected explanation and the minimal repaired defect. A debugger can show a particular state without proving all paths reach that state safely.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-12-a"></a>


- **T32.12.a** Use debugger state, watchpoints, and backtraces to test hypotheses. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-12-b"></a>


- **T32.12.b** Minimize examples before changing multiple variables. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-12-c"></a>


- **T32.12.c** Diagnose optimized and concurrent failures with appropriate caution. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-13"></a>

### T32.13 — Host, simulator, and target evidence

Allocate evidence by modeled behavior: host logic for grammar/ownership, an identified emulator for its implemented core/board behavior, and real hardware for physical bus, analog and timing properties. The same bytes can be reused across these environments while the expected observation differs. Build an evidence matrix and deliberately reject a simulated ADC-accuracy claim. Passing all host fixtures does not close the board-specific obligations.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-13-a"></a>


- **T32.13.a** Allocate tests according to the behavior each environment models. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-13-b"></a>


- **T32.13.b** Keep hardware timing and analog claims outside unsupported simulations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-13-c"></a>


- **T32.13.c** Reuse vectors while preserving target-specific expectations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-14"></a>

### T32.14 — Regression and reproducibility

Regression artifacts are a replay package: exact input, expected relation, binary/symbol identity, versions, flags, command, seed and limitations. Automate a representative debug/release/instrumented matrix and preserve failures before repairing code. Logs from a different image can mislead diagnosis. Evidence must link each claimed property to its test/proof/measurement artifact and show that a fresh replay reproduces both an injected failure and its repaired result.

Apply this mechanism in [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t32-14-a"></a>


- **T32.14.a** Retain failing inputs, binaries, logs, and configuration manifests. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-14-b"></a>


- **T32.14.b** Automate representative build and execution matrices. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).


<a id="t32-14-c"></a>


- **T32.14.c** Make every claimed property traceable to evidence and known limitations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T32-07](#pr-t32-07).

## Reading guidance

Read the bounded selections before the corresponding project, then annotate one contract or assumption you will test. The assigned reading table is generated from the exact inspected locators. Spend the remaining reading budget on original teaching, worked traces and target documentation comparisons, not whole uninspected chapters.

**Test-Driven Development for Embedded C — 5.4 The Embedded TDD Cycle (1 h):** Separate harness/target evidence.

**GCC program instrumentation options, selected verification and hardening contracts — -fsanitize=address (1 h):** Scope exercised memory checks.

**GCC program instrumentation options, selected verification and hardening contracts — -fsanitize=undefined (1 h):** Select arithmetic/semantic diagnostics.

**Valgrind Memcheck manual, selected detection contracts — 4.2.2. Use of uninitialised values (1 h):** Compare initialized-value detection.

**GCC program instrumentation options, selected verification and hardening contracts — -fcondition-coverage (1 h):** Build a targeted independent-effect exercise.

**The Eva plug-in — 1.2 Run-time errors and the absence thereof (1 h):** Interpret static/runtime claims.

**Shared scope limit — Test-Driven Development for Embedded C:** Host tests and simulator runs do not establish actual peripheral behavior. Historical tooling references require current commands. This inspection supports the strategy passages, not all mock-driver chapters.

**Shared scope limit — GCC program instrumentation options, selected verification and hardening contracts:** Selected options only, not every instrumentation feature. Flag availability and effective dependencies vary with installed compiler/target. GNU/Linux hardening aggregate is not a bare-metal recipe; instrumentation changes resource/timing behavior.

**Shared scope limit — Valgrind Memcheck manual, selected detection contracts:** Moving manual snapshot; installed version/platform must be recorded. No tool executed during research. Tool detection does not establish full correctness or prevent the underlying invalid access.

**Shared scope limit — The Eva plug-in:** False alarms can result from approximation. Soundness is relative to the specified context and supported semantics. Current manual states asynchronous interrupts are not directly modeled; do not claim full firmware proof from sequential analysis.

See [guide-reading](#guide-reading) for access/provenance and [guide-standards](#guide-standards) for the language baseline.

## Mastery gate and feedback

Demonstrate an independent oracle, minimized failure, rollback coverage, supported instrumentation comparison and targeted MC/DC pairs. Kill one meaningful mutation and justify one equivalent case. If a failure survives, improve the property/oracle rather than merely increasing random iterations.

For every linked objective, retain a separately labeled explanation, implementation/analysis artifact and check. Use [guide-assessment](#guide-assessment) for the rubric; one passing fixture does not establish all three objectives of a topic.

## Consolidation and transfer

After a delay, substitute a different adapter and replay the retained corpus/matrix. Predict which evidence remains portable and which must be recollected on the OS or physical board.

<!-- enhancement handoff -->

Apply the existing length, arithmetic, ownership and failure reasoning to [T40](#t40)–[T42](#t42). Preserve malformed-input and resource-exhaustion cases at each layer; CRC success and a cooperative peer do not establish authentication or general protocol conformance.

## Environment and limits

Use [guide-profiles](#guide-profiles) to declare the dependency boundary, [guide-laboratory](#guide-laboratory) for installed tools and hardware, and [guide-audit](#guide-audit) for image/call-graph evidence. Fixtures are original deterministic mathematical or synthetic-protocol data. Run `python tools/verify_embedded_fixtures.py` from the curriculum root to recompute their expectations. This oracle checks fixtures, not learner code.

Record host/tool/ISA identities and all mathematical/environment assumptions. Instrumented timings are not production timings; numerical references have stated domains; proof results hold only for reported obligations/models.

Use [guide-inventory](#guide-inventory) to find supplied data and [guide-integrations](#guide-integrations) for later cross-module work.

# T14 — Data structures implemented from first principles

## Purpose and outcomes

Build representations yourself, with ownership and failure semantics established before mutations. The T18 ownership/API work is a hard prerequisite: capacity, iterator invalidation and cleanup are part of each container contract. The intended result is a mechanism you can explain, a bounded artifact you can inspect and an evidence trail someone else can reproduce. The published workload includes 10 h of explicitly elective project work; a core-only route subtracts those project hours, without removing core awareness.

## Entry check and remediation

Produce a T18 ownership table covering creator, borrower, mutator and destroyer; prove one checked size multiplication. Remediate T04 arithmetic and T03 object lifetimes before any container allocation. T18 API and ownership work is required first, including failure effects and borrow invalidation. Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for diagnostic evidence and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route choices. Domain numbers are coverage IDs, not an instruction to study them numerically.

## Study sequence and teaching

Work through the mechanism notes in order within each project, alternating hand prediction with observation. Preserve the first counterexample rather than only a final green test. Full implementations belong to the projects; these notes explain what they must establish.


<a id="t14-01"></a>

### T14.01 — Representation contracts

A container represents logical contents with storage and metadata. Its valid states, borrow lifetimes and mutation permissions belong to the interface before algorithms are chosen.

Storage legality is part of acceptance. Under the selected C17 baseline, an aligned declared unsigned-char array is still a declared character array; alignment alone does not license arbitrary T* lvalue access. The portable byte arena uses byte APIs and explicit copying into/out of actual typed objects. A typed pool uses a real array of the selected T. A hosted harness may separately supply genuine allocated storage through a backing callback, while the studied allocator/container policy stays local. Firmware casts or mapping-backed typed objects need an explicit, inspected implementation contract and are reported under that contract, not as a blanket ISO C guarantee. Check effective type, alignment, bounds and lifetime independently.

Investigate: Write empty/full/destroyed state transitions and an ownership table before implementing any mutation. A common mistake is: A non-null pointer always denotes a valid live container. Evidence: Invariant checks distinguish valid empty storage, exhaustion and destroyed handles. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-01](#pr-t14-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t14-02"></a>

### T14.02 — Fixed arrays and views

A slice borrows a range; it does not own or extend its storage lifetime. Insertion must account for capacity and overlapping movement, while a strided view changes address calculations.

Investigate: Implement bounded insertion/erase and a strided view over caller storage. A common mistake is: A view remains valid after its owner reallocates. Evidence: Boundary and overlap vectors plus an invalidation table justify every access. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-01](#pr-t14-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-02-a"></a>

<a id="t14-02-b"></a>


- **T14.02.b** Compare owning storage with non-owning slices and strided views. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-01](#pr-t14-01).


<a id="t14-02-c"></a>


- **T14.02.c** Prove capacity and overlap requirements for each operation. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-01](#pr-t14-01).


<a id="t14-03"></a>

### T14.03 — Dynamic arrays

Dynamic growth trades spare capacity for fewer relocations. Doubling gives an amortized argument, not a promise about one append; reserve failure must retain the old allocation and contents.

Investigate: Implement reserve/append/insertion with an allocator callback that fails at each acquisition point. A common mistake is: Amortized constant append means every append is constant time. Evidence: A growth-cost ledger and failure snapshots preserve ownership and expose invalidated borrows. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-02](#pr-t14-02).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-03-a"></a>


- **T14.03.a** Implement growth, reserve, shrink, append, and insertion policies. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-02](#pr-t14-02).


<a id="t14-03-b"></a>


- **T14.03.b** Analyze amortized costs and reallocation-induced invalidation. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-02](#pr-t14-02).


<a id="t14-03-c"></a>


- **T14.03.c** Preserve defined state under allocation failure. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-02](#pr-t14-02).


<a id="t14-04"></a>

### T14.04 — Linked structures

List edges encode ownership and reachability. A sentinel simplifies endpoint cases, while an intrusive node belongs to its containing object and cannot be freed as an independent wrapper.

Investigate: Implement singly and doubly linked variants and verify both directions after every removal. A common mistake is: Unlinking a node automatically destroys its payload. Evidence: Head/tail and bidirectional link checks cover first, last, singleton and repeated removal cases. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-03](#pr-t14-03).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-04-a"></a>


- **T14.04.a** Implement singly and doubly linked lists with sentinel alternatives. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-03](#pr-t14-03).


<a id="t14-04-b"></a>


- **T14.04.b** Verify link consistency, removal, and iterator behavior. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-03](#pr-t14-03).


<a id="t14-04-c"></a>


- **T14.04.c** Compare intrusive nodes with separately allocated wrapper nodes. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-03](#pr-t14-03).


<a id="t14-05"></a>

### T14.05 — Stacks, queues, and deques

Stack, queue and deque behavior specifies which logical end is accessed, independently of array or linked representation. Overflow and batch insertion need atomicity or a documented partial-success policy.

Investigate: Implement bounded stack/deque operations and compare a linked queue under the same logical trace. A common mistake is: Queue semantics determine its allocation strategy. Evidence: Reference contents and operation counts agree while exhaustion leaves the declared state unchanged. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-03](#pr-t14-03).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t14-06"></a>

### T14.06 — Ring buffers

A ring uses modular positions but needs a convention to distinguish full from empty. With capacity C and a count, occupied slots can wrap into two spans without moving data.

Investigate: Implement split-span bulk push/pop using caller storage. A common mistake is: Equal head and tail always means empty. Evidence: Wrap vectors reconstruct logical FIFO order and prove available/free counts at every transition. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-01](#pr-t14-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t14-06-b"></a>


- **T14.06.b** Implement wraparound, split spans, and bulk transfers. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-01](#pr-t14-01).

<a id="t14-07"></a>

### T14.07 — Hash tables

Chaining stores collision groups explicitly; open addressing probes through them. A tombstone preserves reachability after deletion, while an empty slot can terminate a failed search.

Investigate: Implement one chained and one linear-probing table with deliberate colliding immutable keys. A common mistake is: Deleting a probed key can turn its slot directly into empty. Evidence: Collision/tombstone traces and failure-injected rehashes preserve every remaining key. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-04](#pr-t14-04).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t14-08"></a>

### T14.08 — Heaps and priority queues

A heap stores a partial order rather than a fully sorted sequence. Children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 require checked bounds before arithmetic; equal priorities need a declared tie policy.

Investigate: Implement bottom-up build, insertion and extraction with an explicit update-key exclusion or handle scheme. A common mistake is: A heap array is globally sorted. Evidence: Parent-child invariants and extraction order match a multiset oracle, including ties. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-05](#pr-t14-05).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t14-09"></a>

### T14.09 — Search trees

An ordered tree separates ordering from parent/child ownership. Two-child deletion replaces or moves a successor, so iterator and payload lifetimes cannot be inferred from key equality.

Investigate: Implement search, insertion, all deletion shapes and explicit-stack traversal. A common mistake is: Deleting a key always frees the exact node originally returned by search. Evidence: Sorted traversal, reachability and parent-link checks agree after each mutation. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-05](#pr-t14-05).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-09-a"></a>


- **T14.09.a** Implement ordered search, insertion, deletion, and traversal. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-05](#pr-t14-05).


<a id="t14-09-b"></a>


- **T14.09.b** Compare recursive and explicit-stack operations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-05](#pr-t14-05).


<a id="t14-09-c"></a>


- **T14.09.c** Track parent links, ownership, and mutation invalidation. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-05](#pr-t14-05).


<a id="t14-10"></a>

### T14.10 — Balanced trees

AVL balance limits the difference between child heights. Rotations preserve in-order contents but update local links/heights; deletion may require repairing several ancestors.

Worked AVL repair: choose height(empty)=0 and height(leaf)=1, and balance=height(left)-height(right). Inserting 30,20,10 first makes root 30 left-heavy with balance +2. Rotate right at 30: root becomes 20 with leaf children 10 and 30; their heights are 1 and the root height is 2. Duplicate 20 is rejected with the entire structure unchanged. Deleting leaf 30 leaves root 20, left child 10, height 2 and balance +1; ancestor checks still run. More demanding deletion orders can decrease heights through several ancestors, so this anchor does not justify insertion-style early stopping.

Investigate: Implement a complete AVL family with LL, RR, LR, RL and cascading deletion tests. A common mistake is: Insertion rotations alone complete a balanced-tree implementation. Evidence: Every node has correct stored height and balance at most one after exhaustive small-key permutations. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-06](#pr-t14-06).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-10-a"></a>


- **T14.10.a** Implement one AVL or red-black family completely. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-06](#pr-t14-06).


<a id="t14-10-b"></a>


- **T14.10.b** Test rotations, rebalancing, and deletion corner cases. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-06](#pr-t14-06).

<a id="t14-11"></a>

### T14.11 — Tries and prefix indexes

A byte trie consumes key units along edges and marks terminal keys separately from prefixes. Empty and embedded-zero keys need explicit length semantics; compression changes memory layout without changing lookup meaning.

Investigate: Implement a length-delimited trie, then compare its node cost with a sketched radix representation. A common mistake is: An internal node automatically denotes a stored key. Evidence: Prefix enumeration and exact membership distinguish empty key, prefix-only path and full key. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-07](#pr-t14-07).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t14-12"></a>

### T14.12 — Bitsets and sparse sets

Dense bitsets pay for the universe; sparse sets pay for present members plus an index. Generation-based clearing avoids immediate writes but introduces wraparound and stale-generation obligations.

Investigate: Implement bounded bitset algebra and a sparse set with insertion/deletion/iteration. A common mistake is: Fast clear can ignore generation wraparound forever. Evidence: Set-algebra oracles, storage totals and clearing-cost measurements include an explicit wrap/reset policy. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-07](#pr-t14-07).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-12-a"></a>


- **T14.12.a** Implement bit operations, iteration, and set algebra. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-07](#pr-t14-07).


<a id="t14-12-b"></a>


- **T14.12.b** Compare dense, sparse, and generation-based representations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-07](#pr-t14-07).


<a id="t14-12-c"></a>

<a id="t14-13"></a>

### T14.13 — Disjoint sets and graphs

Union-find represents equivalence classes using roots; path compression rewrites paths but preserves partitions. Graph storage is a different abstraction: adjacency lists, matrices and compressed rows answer different access patterns.

Investigate: Implement union-by-size with compression and convert a fixed graph among three representations. A common mistake is: A union-find parent edge is an original graph edge. Evidence: Partition checks and normalized edge sets agree after unions and representation conversion. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-08](#pr-t14-08).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-13-a"></a>


- **T14.13.a** Implement union-find with documented optimization invariants. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-08](#pr-t14-08).


<a id="t14-13-b"></a>


- **T14.13.b** Build adjacency-list, matrix, and compressed graph representations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-08](#pr-t14-08).


<a id="t14-13-c"></a>


- **T14.13.c** Separate representation operations from graph algorithms in T15. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-08](#pr-t14-08).


<a id="t14-14"></a>

### T14.14 — Advanced structures

An advanced structure earns its complexity through a workload and a precise promise. Skip-list randomness or probabilistic filters do not create deterministic worst-case guarantees by themselves. This topic is elective; its implementation project is optional.

Investigate: Choose a skip list, B-tree or membership filter and retain a simple exact model. A common mistake is: A probabilistic membership hit proves the key is present. Evidence: The elective report separates false-positive/ordering guarantees, resource costs and implementation evidence. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-09](#pr-t14-09).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t14-14-a"></a>

<a id="t14-14-b"></a>


- **T14.14.b** Implement a selected structure for a concrete workload. **Disposition:** elective. **Activity:** [PR-T14-09](#pr-t14-09).

### T14.15 — Container verification

A mutation test must compare logical contents and representation invariants, especially after failure. A benchmark answers workload costs, while asymptotic reasoning explains scaling.

Investigate: Generate short operation sequences and check invariants after every operation and allocator failure. A common mistake is: A final correct result excuses transient ownership corruption. Evidence: Minimized traces preserve the earliest broken invariant and benchmark setup discloses distributions and instrumentation. Develop that evidence in [PR-T14-02](#pr-t14-02).


#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

- **T14.15.b** Check invariants after every operation and injected failure. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T14-02](#pr-t14-02).

## Reading guidance

The essential spine below is deliberately narrow. Assign only the exact inspected registry locators shown; no whole book, standard or implementation is implied. Historical rationale does not replace a current contract, and one implementation does not create a portable guarantee. Keep a short discrepancy log linking each source claim to the target/configuration where it applies.

- **C Interfaces and Implementations: Techniques for Creating Reusable Software (First edition)** — `R-hanson-cii`, exactly **3.1 Interface** (1 h). Use Hanson’s atom interface to study owned/interned storage and borrower lifetime boundaries. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.
- **Open Data Structures (in C++) (Online edition 0.1f)** — `R-morin-ods-0-1f`, exactly **5.2 LinearHashTable: Linear Probing** (1 h). Trace probe reachability through linear-probing search, insertion and deletion. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as supplement; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.
- **Introduction to Algorithms (Fourth edition)** — `R-clrs-4`, exactly **13.1 Properties of red-black trees** (1 h). Compare red-black balance policy with the implemented AVL height invariant; do not copy its repair rules into AVL. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

See [guide-reading](#guide-reading) and [guide-standards](#guide-standards) for edition and evidence distinctions. Additional elective/API investigations require inspecting their precise version-specific passages before treating them as assigned authority.

## Mastery gate and feedback

Explain one positive path and one failure/counterexample for every subtopic without reading your implementation. Submit each project’s leaf-objective checklist with a distinct evidence item; shared runs may support several items only when the relation is explained. Re-run the saved independent fixture verifier, then reproduce at least one artifact from a clean environment. Passing those checks is evidence within their scope, not full-domain certification.

If an invariant, lifetime or environment claim cannot be defended, return to its project’s smallest trace and remediate the named entry knowledge. If a tool result disagrees with reasoning, minimize before changing expected results. A module passes when all core projects and awareness duties are accepted; elective implementation gaps remain visible. Use [guide-assessment](#guide-assessment) and [guide-audit](#guide-audit) for review records.

## Consolidation and transfer

After at least one day, reconstruct a selected contract and failing trace from memory, then apply one changed capacity/backend/target assumption. Explain which evidence survives and which must be regenerated. Transfer the dependency, ownership, representation or ordering ledger into the next project rather than copying an unexplained implementation. Record the delayed correction in the consolidation budget; see [guide-integrations](#guide-integrations) and [guide-workload](#guide-workload).

<!-- enhancement handoff -->

Carry the existing typed container, ownership and invalidation contracts into [T36](#t36). Derive the new invariant or representation alternative before changing the implementation; retain the original project evidence rather than rebuilding every container.

## Environment and limits

Use the declared Linux x86-64 environment for hosted observations and profile-specific adapters for portable components. Record compiler, linker, OS/library, architecture and configuration. Synthetic fixtures certify their declared static/reference calculations only. Unavailable target runs, unsupported instrumentation and hardware-dependent results are reported explicitly; emulator results do not prove STM32 electrical/peripheral behavior. No privileged host operation is required by a core project. See [guide-laboratory](#guide-laboratory), [guide-profiles](#guide-profiles) and [guide-inventory](#guide-inventory) before changing a boundary.

## Purpose and outcomes

Implement algorithms and parsers under caller-workspace and no-external-library constraints. Connect invariants and resource bounds to independently checked cases, including duplicates, overflow and arbitrary chunk boundaries. The intended result is a mechanism you can explain, a bounded artifact you can inspect and an evidence trail someone else can reproduce. The published workload includes 10 h of explicitly elective project work; a core-only route subtracts those project hours, without removing core awareness.

## Entry check and remediation

Check the invariants and workspace contract of the T14 fixed array/ring, then trace a half-open search. Repair representation correctness before attributing failures to algorithms. Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for diagnostic evidence and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route choices. Domain numbers are coverage IDs, not an instruction to study them numerically.

## Study sequence and teaching

Work through the mechanism notes in order within each project, alternating hand prediction with observation. Preserve the first counterexample rather than only a final green test. Full implementations belong to the projects; these notes explain what they must establish.


<a id="t15-01"></a>

### T15.01 — Search and partition

Binary search narrows a half-open interval while preserving a relation to the answer. lower_bound finds the first value not less than a key; upper_bound finds the first greater value.

Investigate: Implement both bounds and partition with lo+(hi−lo)/2 and explicit empty-range handling. A common mistake is: Any matching index is a correct lower bound. Evidence: Duplicate and empty-range cases match a linear oracle and each update preserves the stated invariant. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-01](#pr-t15-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t15-01-a"></a>


- **T15.01.a** Implement linear search, binary search, and lower/upper bounds. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T15-01](#pr-t15-01).


<a id="t15-01-b"></a>


- **T15.01.b** Prove loop invariants and empty-range behavior. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T15-01](#pr-t15-01).


<a id="t15-01-c"></a>


- **T15.01.c** Implement partitioning without overflow-prone midpoint or index calculations. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T15-01](#pr-t15-01).


<a id="t15-02"></a>

### T15.02 — Elementary and comparison sorting

Insertion sort supplies a small stable reference; merge sort trades temporary storage for stable merging; heap sort supplies a comparison bound with different locality. Stability concerns equal-key identity.

Worked stable merge: sorted left [1A,3A] and right [1B,2B] have labeled equal keys. Taking the left element on equality produces [1A,1B,2B,3A], preserving the earlier 1A; taking the right equal key would violate stability. A four-element caller workspace receives one element per transition, and the two input cursors never pass their lengths. For heap sort, reuse PR-T14-05 build/sift-down: max-heap [4,3,2,1] has active length 4. Swap root with the final active element to obtain [1,3,2 | 4], shrink to 3, then sift to [3,1,2 | 4]. Next extraction gives [2,1 | 3,4]; the active root already dominates its child. The last exchange gives [1 | 2,3,4]. Each step preserves the active max-heap and increasing final suffix; heap sort has no stable-tie promise.

Investigate: Implement all three using caller storage and labeled equal keys. A common mistake is: Sorting equal values proves stability. Evidence: Results preserve the multiset; labeled ties, comparison counts and scratch-space budgets expose the differences. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-01](#pr-t15-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t15-02-b"></a>

### T15.03 — Quicksort and hybrid sorting

Quicksort partitions around pivots but can degenerate under adversarial choices. Three-way partitioning groups duplicates; smaller-side recursion and a depth-limited fallback constrain stack/work.

Investigate: Implement a duplicate-aware quicksort with a justified heap-sort fallback. A common mistake is: Random-looking input proves a worst-case bound. Evidence: Sorted/reverse/equal-key vectors plus depth and comparison counters exercise the fallback. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-02](#pr-t15-02).

#### Evidence checklist

### T15.04 — Counting and radix methods

Counting sorts allocate by key range rather than item count; radix passes compose a stable digit order. Signed keys need an order-preserving mapping before unsigned digit extraction.

Investigate: Implement counting sort and least-significant-digit radix sort over a declared bounded integer domain. A common mistake is: Unsigned byte order automatically matches signed numerical order. Evidence: Negative/positive endpoints, stability and auxiliary-storage totals agree with a numeric oracle. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-03](#pr-t15-03).

#### Evidence checklist

### T15.05 — Selection and order statistics

Selection needs only a rank boundary, not a fully sorted array. Duplicate partitions can contain the requested rank; invalid ranks must fail before reading storage.

Investigate: Implement quickselect with a three-way partition and state its expected and worst-case behavior. A common mistake is: Quickselect always has deterministic linear worst-case cost. Evidence: Every valid rank equals a sorted-reference value, and invalid ranks leave inputs under the declared failure policy. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-02](#pr-t15-02).

### T15.06 — String matching

Naive matching compares at each candidate position. A prefix/failure table reuses information about matched prefixes to avoid restarting work; byte spans do not require a terminator.

Investigate: Implement naive and prefix-function matching with overlapping matches and embedded-zero input. A common mistake is: A zero byte necessarily ends the search input. Evidence: Match offsets agree with direct bounded comparisons and the linear method reports bounded fallback work. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-04](#pr-t15-04).

BFS discovers layers in an unweighted graph; DFS follows depth and records visitation state. Explicit work storage makes recursion and its resource bound visible.

<a id="t15-08"></a>

### T15.08 — Graph ordering and paths

Topological order exists only for a directed acyclic graph. Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights; Bellman-Ford can detect a reachable negative cycle. Unweighted shortest paths need neither weighted algorithm.

Investigate: Implement topological cycle detection and a bounded nonnegative shortest-path solver; analyze a negative-edge counterexample. A common mistake is: Dijkstra remains valid whenever there is no negative cycle. Evidence: Every reported path has valid edges and cost, and violated weight assumptions fail explicitly. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-05](#pr-t15-05).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t15-09"></a>

### T15.09 — Greedy and dynamic programming

A greedy choice needs an exchange argument that replacing an optimum choice does not harm feasibility. Dynamic programming names a state, recurrence and evaluation order; in-place compression can overwrite a needed previous layer.

Worked recurrence trap: with one 0/1 item of weight 2 and value 3, capacity 4 admits value 3. Updating capacities upwards lets the same row’s value at capacity 2 feed capacity 4, incorrectly yielding 6 and using the item twice. Descending updates preserve the prior-item dependency; exhaustive subsets independently establish the correct tiny result.

Investigate: Implement interval scheduling and bounded 0/1 knapsack with a descending capacity update. A common mistake is: An ascending 0/1 knapsack loop preserves the same item-use contract. Evidence: A brute-force subset oracle checks tiny instances and exposes unintended repeated item use. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-06](#pr-t15-06).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

### T15.10 — Byte primitives and spans

A span is a pointer plus a length, with a borrow lifetime and aliasing contract. Copy, search, split and trim should report bounds and output capacity independently of NUL termination.

Investigate: Implement a shared byte-span kernel without libc calls and connect it to the T11 support boundary. A common mistake is: A split operation can retain pointers after backing storage dies. Evidence: Zero-length, delimiter-only, overlap and exact-capacity vectors check both semantics and dependency closure. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-07](#pr-t15-07).

### T15.11 — Numeric parsing and formatting

Checked parsing accumulates only after proving the next digit fits: value≤(limit−digit)/base. A signed minimum magnitude must be represented without overflowing a signed negation.

A common mistake is: atoi-style conversion can diagnose overflow or incomplete input. Evidence: Limit−1, limit, limit+1 and minimum-value vectors agree with arbitrary-precision arithmetic. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-07](#pr-t15-07).

### T15.12 — Serialization and integrity

Serialization chooses byte order and field widths independently of host layout. A CRC is a parameterized polynomial computation, so a test vector must name reflection, initialization and final XOR.

Investigate: Encode a tiny versioned record and CRC-8/0x07 message checksum using byte operations. A common mistake is: Copying a C structure creates a portable wire format. Evidence: Known vectors, endian-independent round trips and reserved-bit rejection match a bit-polynomial oracle. Develop that evidence in [PR-T15-08](#pr-t15-08).

### T15.13 — Framing and incremental parsing

An incremental parser preserves state across arbitrary chunk boundaries and distinguishes incomplete input from malformed input. Length and nesting limits also bound recovery work and queued storage.

## Reading guidance

The essential spine below is deliberately narrow. Assign only the exact inspected registry locators shown; no whole book, standard or implementation is implied. Historical rationale does not replace a current contract, and one implementation does not create a portable guarantee. Keep a short discrepancy log linking each source claim to the target/configuration where it applies.

- **Introduction to Algorithms (Fourth edition)** — `R-clrs-4`, exactly **Loop invariants and the correctness of insertion sort** (1 h). Use insertion-sort loop invariants to structure correctness arguments for each implementation. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.
- **Crafting Interpreters (Online author manuscript; chapter Scanning on Demand)** — `R-nystrom-scanner`, exactly **A Token at a Time** (1 h). Trace token-at-a-time scanning and explicit input/lexeme boundaries. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as supplement; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.
- **An Axiomatic Basis for Computer Programming (Communications of the ACM 12(10))** — `R-hoare-axiomatic-1969`, exactly **3.4. Rule of Iteration** (1 h). Apply iteration reasoning to a decreasing loop measure and preserved invariant. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

See [guide-reading](#guide-reading) and [guide-standards](#guide-standards) for edition and evidence distinctions. Additional elective/API investigations require inspecting their precise version-specific passages before treating them as assigned authority.

## Mastery gate and feedback

Explain one positive path and one failure/counterexample for every subtopic without reading your implementation. Submit each project’s leaf-objective checklist with a distinct evidence item; shared runs may support several items only when the relation is explained. Re-run the saved independent fixture verifier, then reproduce at least one artifact from a clean environment. Passing those checks is evidence within their scope, not full-domain certification.

If an invariant, lifetime or environment claim cannot be defended, return to its project’s smallest trace and remediate the named entry knowledge. If a tool result disagrees with reasoning, minimize before changing expected results. A module passes when all core projects and awareness duties are accepted; elective implementation gaps remain visible. Use [guide-assessment](#guide-assessment) and [guide-audit](#guide-audit) for review records.

## Consolidation and transfer

After at least one day, reconstruct a selected contract and failing trace from memory, then apply one changed capacity/backend/target assumption. Explain which evidence survives and which must be regenerated. Transfer the dependency, ownership, representation or ordering ledger into the next project rather than copying an unexplained implementation. Record the delayed correction in the consolidation budget; see [guide-integrations](#guide-integrations) and [guide-workload](#guide-workload).

## Environment and limits

Use the declared Linux x86-64 environment for hosted observations and profile-specific adapters for portable components. Record compiler, linker, OS/library, architecture and configuration. Synthetic fixtures certify their declared static/reference calculations only. Unavailable target runs, unsupported instrumentation and hardware-dependent results are reported explicitly; emulator results do not prove STM32 electrical/peripheral behavior. No privileged host operation is required by a core project. See [guide-laboratory](#guide-laboratory), [guide-profiles](#guide-profiles) and [guide-inventory](#guide-inventory) before changing a boundary.

## Purpose and outcomes

Make allocation follow object lifetimes and bounded backing storage. Implement local policies rather than delegating to malloc, and preserve ownership under exhaustion, migration and rollback. The intended result is a mechanism you can explain, a bounded artifact you can inspect and an evidence trail someone else can reproduce. The published workload includes 10 h of explicitly elective project work; a core-only route subtracts those project hours, without removing core awareness.

## Entry check and remediation

State allocate/resize failure ownership and compute an aligned offset with checked addition. Explain why an aligned declared byte array is not automatically generic typed-object storage in C17. Repeat T18 API/ownership, T03 effective type/lifetime and T04 checked arithmetic before implementing policy if any boundary is unclear. Use [guide-entry](#guide-entry) for diagnostic evidence and [guide-roadmap](#guide-roadmap) for route choices. Domain numbers are coverage IDs, not an instruction to study them numerically.

## Study sequence and teaching

Work through the mechanism notes in order within each project, alternating hand prediction with observation. Preserve the first counterexample rather than only a final green test. Full implementations belong to the projects; these notes explain what they must establish.


<a id="t16-01"></a>

### T16.01 — Allocator contracts

An allocator acquires storage; it does not initialize application objects. Allocate, release and resize need contracts for alignment, zero size, exhaustion and who owns the old object after failure.

Storage legality is part of acceptance. Under the selected C17 baseline, an aligned declared unsigned-char array is still a declared character array; alignment alone does not license arbitrary T* lvalue access. The portable byte arena uses byte APIs and explicit copying into/out of actual typed objects. A typed pool uses a real array of the selected T. A hosted harness may separately supply genuine allocated storage through a backing callback, while the studied allocator/container policy stays local. Firmware casts or mapping-backed typed objects need an explicit, inspected implementation contract and are reported under that contract, not as a blanket ISO C guarantee. Check effective type, alignment, bounds and lifetime independently.

Investigate: Write an allocator callback interface and a transition table before choosing a policy. A common mistake is: An allocator return automatically contains a valid initialized object. Evidence: Zero-size and exhaustion cases have one documented result and ownership remains unambiguous. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t16-01-a"></a>


- **T16.01.a** Specify allocate, deallocate, resize, and alignment semantics. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-01-b"></a>


- **T16.01.b** Define zero-size requests, exhaustion, ownership, and supported lifetimes. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-01-c"></a>

<a id="t16-02"></a>

### T16.02 — Layout and checked arithmetic

Alignment adds padding before payload placement. For power-of-two a, padding can be computed as (a−offset%a)%a, then bounds checked before addition. Metadata and minimum fragment sizes consume capacity too.

Investigate: Calculate layouts for several requests near the end of a fixed region using checked size arithmetic. A common mistake is: Rounding an already overflowing sum repairs overflow. Evidence: Payload, padding, headers and remaining capacity reconcile exactly; unsupported alignment fails before mutation. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t16-02-a"></a>


- **T16.02.a** Calculate aligned offsets without overflowing intermediate arithmetic. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-02-b"></a>


- **T16.02.b** Separate requested payload from headers, padding, and usable capacity. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-02-c"></a>


- **T16.02.c** Verify metadata alignment and minimum block sizes. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-03"></a>

### T16.03 — Bump and arena allocation

A bump arena advances a cursor through caller-owned storage and reclaims a whole lifetime region at reset. Reset invalidates every borrowed object in that region, even if its bytes are unchanged.

Worked arena accounting: with cursor 3, size 5 and alignment 8, padding is 5, so the allocation begins at offset 8 and ends at 13. A later ten-byte request aligned to 4 would end at 26 and must fail in a 24-byte region, preserving cursor 13. A one-byte alignment-1 request can then succeed at 13. Count padding as charged storage, and check additions before forming any pointer.

Investigate: Implement an aligned arena with high-water tracking and generation-marked debug handles. A common mistake is: An arena reset preserves live pointers because memory was not freed to the OS. Evidence: Allocation traces never overlap, satisfy alignment and identify all invalidated handles after reset. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.


<a id="t16-03-a"></a>


- **T16.03.a** Implement allocation from caller-owned contiguous storage. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-03-b"></a>


- **T16.03.b** Support explicit reset with invalidation of all affected objects. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-03-c"></a>


- **T16.03.c** Compare high-water usage with total requested payload. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-01](#pr-t16-01).


<a id="t16-04"></a>

### T16.04 — Checkpoints and temporary regions

A mark records a rollback boundary, not an independent allocation owner. Nested temporary regions must close in order, and an escaped borrow can outlive the storage it names.

Investigate: Implement nested marks with generation/order checks and a deliberate escaped-reference test. A common mistake is: Rollback is safe whenever the cursor can be restored numerically. Evidence: Out-of-order rollback is rejected and a lifetime diagram distinguishes surviving and invalidated objects. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-02](#pr-t16-02).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-04-b"></a>

<a id="t16-04-c"></a>

<a id="t16-05"></a>

### T16.05 — Stack allocation

A stack allocator reclaims the most recent block using explicit metadata. That storage policy does not run application cleanup, and it is unrelated to the compiler stack merely because both are LIFO.

Investigate: Implement release with a top-block token and separate cleanup callbacks. A common mistake is: Reclaiming bytes disposes of resources held by the object. Evidence: Non-top releases fail without state change and exactly-once cleanup evidence is separate from byte accounting. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-02](#pr-t16-02).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-05-b"></a>


- **T16.05.b** Compare stack allocators with language automatic storage. **Disposition:** core. **Activity:** [PR-T16-02](#pr-t16-02).


<a id="t16-05-c"></a>

<a id="t16-06"></a>

### T16.06 — Fixed-block pools

A fixed pool divides storage into aligned slots and tracks free membership. Generation handles detect reuse only while the generation scheme remains meaningful; raw stale pointers bypass that protection.

Investigate: Implement a pool bitmap plus index/generation handles and exhaustion/double-release tests. A common mistake is: A reused slot address has the same object identity. Evidence: The ownership model rejects stale handles and reports a generation-wrap policy. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-03](#pr-t16-03).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-06-b"></a>

<a id="t16-07"></a>

### T16.07 — Variable-size free lists

A free-list policy chooses among holes. Splitting must leave either a usable remainder or absorb the tail; searching faster and fragmenting less are different goals.

Investigate: Implement first-fit with a declared minimum remainder and adversarial request traces. A common mistake is: Total free bytes guarantees one request can be served. Evidence: Largest-free-block and search-step evidence explain failures despite adequate total free space. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-04](#pr-t16-04).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-08"></a>

### T16.08 — Boundary tags and coalescing

Boundary metadata lets an allocator locate adjacent blocks for coalescing. Updating tags and list membership must be one coherent mutation so traversal never sees overlapping free extents.

Investigate: Add boundary tags and left/right/both-neighbor merge cases, checking the heap after every step. A common mistake is: Merging adjacent bytes alone completes free-list repair. Evidence: Ordered block extents, boundary tags and free-list membership agree after all merge orders. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-04](#pr-t16-04).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-08-b"></a>

<a id="t16-09"></a>

### T16.09 — Segregated classes and slabs

Size classes reduce search and group similar objects but round requests upward. A slab with one live slot still retains its backing storage, and reuse requires reinitialization of object state.

Investigate: Implement two fixed size classes and calculate internal waste and partial-slab occupancy. A common mistake is: Freed cached objects are already initialized for their next owner. Evidence: Per-class capacity, retained bytes and reinitialization tests distinguish cache storage from live payload. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-05](#pr-t16-05).

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-09-b"></a>

<a id="t16-09-c"></a>

<a id="t16-10"></a>

### T16.10 — Buddy and real-time-oriented allocation

Buddy splitting constrains sizes to powers of two; a buddy is found by toggling the relevant address bit only within the correctly aligned region. Algorithmic bounds do not cover interrupt interference or cache misses. This topic is elective; its implementation project is optional.

Investigate: Implement a small elective buddy allocator or analyze pinned TLSF source after additional inspection. A common mistake is: Constant-time indexing proves a complete hard real-time latency bound. Evidence: Split/merge traces and a separate hardware-assumption list limit any timing claim. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-06](#pr-t16-06).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-11"></a>

### T16.11 — Resize and migration

Resize can retain location or migrate contents. On failure the original ownership remains; after a successful move aliases and iterators to the old block become invalid. Shrink must respect metadata/minimum fragment rules.

Investigate: Implement move-resize with injected allocation failure, then add one justified in-place policy. A common mistake is: A failed resize frees the old object. Evidence: Snapshot contents and identity are preserved on failure; successful migration copies only the retained payload. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-07](#pr-t16-07).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-12"></a>

### T16.12 — Backing storage and concurrency

Backing storage and synchronization are independent layers. A mapping supplies bytes to an allocator; a shared allocator lock protects metadata, not every application object stored inside.

Investigate: Adapt an arena to static storage and a declared Linux mapping backend, and compare per-thread ownership with a locked shared policy. A common mistake is: A thread-safe allocator makes allocated objects thread-safe. Evidence: Backend effects and metadata locking are separated from application publication/lifetime arguments. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-08](#pr-t16-08).

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-13"></a>

### T16.13 — Lifetime architecture

Regions should follow real use intervals: per-message, per-frame and persistent objects need different reclamation points. Forcing independently released objects into one arena can retain large amounts of dead storage.

Investigate: Draw object use intervals for a parser/request pipeline and choose region boundaries. A common mistake is: One arena per program is always the simplest efficient lifetime design. Evidence: Peak-live and retained-byte calculations justify the selected regions and the exceptions. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-08](#pr-t16-08).

#### Evidence checklist

Retain a separate evidence item for each objective below. Meeting one objective does not establish the others.

<a id="t16-14"></a>

### T16.14 — Allocator verification

Allocator verification models live extents independently of policy and checks overlap, alignment and ownership after each action. Instrumentation changes latency and sometimes layout, so measurement costs must be disclosed.

Investigate: Generate allocate/free/resize traces with failures and compare against an abstract live-allocation model. A common mistake is: Passing a few throughput runs establishes allocator correctness. Evidence: Minimized corruption traces and separate peak/fragmentation/latency reports support bounded conclusions. Develop that evidence in [PR-T16-09](#pr-t16-09).

## Reading guidance

The essential spine below is deliberately narrow. Assign only the exact inspected registry locators shown; no whole book, standard or implementation is implied. Historical rationale does not replace a current contract, and one implementation does not create a portable guarantee. Keep a short discrepancy log linking each source claim to the target/configuration where it applies.

- **C Interfaces and Implementations: Techniques for Creating Reusable Software (First edition)** — `R-hanson-cii`, exactly **6.1 Interface** (1 h). Read the memory interface’s acquisition/release/failure responsibilities before local allocator policy. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.
- **Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review (1995 survey; public revised preprint)** — `R-wilson-allocation-1995`, exactly **1.3 Strategies, Placement Policies, and Splitting and Coalescing** (1 h). Separate internal/external fragmentation and placement/coalescing choices. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as primary; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.
- **Programming languages — C: working draft N3096 (N3096, April 1, 2023)** — `R-wg14-n3096`, exactly **7.24.3.7 The realloc function** (1 h). Apply the selected C draft’s resize lifetime/failure contract without importing it unchanged into C17. Compare the source claim with your project assumptions. The registry classifies this as oracle; its inspection limits remain part of the assignment.

See [guide-reading](#guide-reading) and [guide-standards](#guide-standards) for edition and evidence distinctions. Additional elective/API investigations require inspecting their precise version-specific passages before treating them as assigned authority.

## Mastery gate and feedback

Explain one positive path and one failure/counterexample for every subtopic without reading your implementation. Submit each project’s leaf-objective checklist with a distinct evidence item; shared runs may support several items only when the relation is explained. Re-run the saved independent fixture verifier, then reproduce at least one artifact from a clean environment. Passing those checks is evidence within their scope, not full-domain certification.

If an invariant, lifetime or environment claim cannot be defended, return to its project’s smallest trace and remediate the named entry knowledge. If a tool result disagrees with reasoning, minimize before changing expected results. A module passes when all core projects and awareness duties are accepted; elective implementation gaps remain visible. Use [guide-assessment](#guide-assessment) and [guide-audit](#guide-audit) for review records.

## Consolidation and transfer

After at least one day, reconstruct a selected contract and failing trace from memory, then apply one changed capacity/backend/target assumption. Explain which evidence survives and which must be regenerated. Transfer the dependency, ownership, representation or ordering ledger into the next project rather than copying an unexplained implementation. Record the delayed correction in the consolidation budget; see [guide-integrations](#guide-integrations) and [guide-workload](#guide-workload).

## Environment and limits

Use the declared Linux x86-64 environment for hosted observations and profile-specific adapters for portable components. Record compiler, linker, OS/library, architecture and configuration. Synthetic fixtures certify their declared static/reference calculations only. Unavailable target runs, unsupported instrumentation and hardware-dependent results are reported explicitly; emulator results do not prove STM32 electrical/peripheral behavior. No privileged host operation is required by a core project. See [guide-laboratory](#guide-laboratory), [guide-profiles](#guide-profiles) and [guide-inventory](#guide-inventory) before changing a boundary.
